title: A Hymn for the Cellar
premise: Wendell Ravensworth, a hospice nurse who has spent seven years hiding in the night shifts of Marrow House, records his dying residents counting backwards in their sleep—and one night, the recordings capture a second voice answering questions it should not know. The voice belongs to Elias Thorne, a resident who vanished from the house's cellar in 1974, and it demands Wendell return what was taken: a ledger of names that proves the home's founders sold residents to a private sanatorium. As Wendell digs into the house's sealed basement, he discovers he was placed at Marrow House deliberately—the last living Thorne, his own memory of childhood erased. In the end, Wendell signs nothing, burns the papers that would erase Elias forever, and lets the house's remaining residents remember aloud, dissolving his invisibility at last as the cellar finally goes quiet.
about_author: Paloma Iversen is a former hospice volunteer from coastal Maine who writes horror about the institutions we trust with our endings. A Hymn for the Cellar is her third novel.

chapters.title: The Counting Hour
chapters.summary: POV Wendell. On his seventh anniversary at Marrow House, Wendell tends to dying resident Agnes, who counts backwards in her sleep—down past zero, into numbers that don't exist. He soothes her with practiced lies about heating pipes for the noises below. Emotional beat: the fragile comfort of routine, and the first hairline crack in it.

chapters.title: Second Voice
chapters.summary: POV Wendell. Reviewing his sleep-recording habit—a private ritual to prove the noises are explainable—Wendell hears a second voice answer Agnes's counting, asking questions only she could answer. It knows her maiden name. He tells himself it's a radio bleed-through. Emotional beat: dread disguised as skepticism.

chapters.title: What Agnes Signed
chapters.summary: POV Wendell. Administrator Dr. Pell pressures the lucid residents to sign 'continuity of care' papers before the home's sale closes in three weeks. Agnes refuses, muttering about 1974 and 'the ledger.' That night the second voice says Wendell's name. Emotional beat: the sense of being watched by something patient.

chapters.title: The Sealed Stair
chapters.summary: POV Wendell. Following the voice's humming—an old hymn—Wendell finds a drywall seam behind the laundry room concealing a stairwell to the cellar, padlocked from the inside. Scratched into the doorframe: dozens of names and dates, all 1974. Emotional beat: curiosity curdling into complicity.

chapters.title: Elias
chapters.summary: POV Wendell, intercut with recorded testimony. The voice identifies itself: Elias Thorne, admitted in 1974, never discharged. Through Agnes's failing memory, Wendell learns residents were sold to the Hollis Sanatorium and their files rewritten. The ledger proving it is still in the cellar. Emotional beat: grief for strangers who were made unpersons.

chapters.title: Ravensworth
chapters.summary: POV Wendell. Digging into his own adoption records, Wendell finds his birth name: Thorne. His mother signed him away in 1974 and had his memories of the house medically blurred. He wasn't hired here—he was returned. Emotional beat: identity collapse; the invisible man discovering he was always the point.

chapters.title: Pell's Hymn
chapters.summary: POV Wendell. Dr. Pell reveals she knows what Wendell has found; her family built the arrangement in 1974, and the sale depends on every signature. She offers him his file—his real history—in exchange for the ledger's destruction. The voice begins singing louder each night. Emotional beat: temptation dressed as mercy.

chapters.title: Down Where the Numbers End
chapters.summary: POV Wendell. Wendell breaks the padlock and descends. The cellar holds the ledger, rows of small beds, and Elias—not a ghost but something sustained by refusal, kept animate by every unsigned paper. Elias shows him the final page: his mother's name, and his own, listed as property. Emotional beat: horror and recognition fused.

chapters.title: The Last Signature
chapters.summary: POV Wendell. Sale day. Pell corners Wendell with the final papers; signing erases the residents' claims and Elias with them. Wendell instead reads the ledger's names aloud over the house intercom while Agnes and the others confirm them, each spoken name loosening the voice's grip on the house. Emotional beat: climax—justice performed as witness, outside any court.

chapters.title: A Hymn for the Cellar
chapters.summary: POV Wendell. The sale collapses; the state opens an inquiry into Hollis. The cellar is silent now, the hymn finished. Wendell, no longer invisible, stays on as the home's nurse under his true name, teaching the residents the hymn so no one is ever forgotten again. Emotional beat: quiet, earned peace—and the cost of being seen.
